title: Research Explained #24 — Why We Try to Break Our Own Architecture First
html:
Why deliberately searching for failures is an essential part of building scientific software we can trust.

Building Something We Can Trust

When most people think about developing software, they probably imagine a fairly straightforward process.

You decide what the software should do. You design it, write the code, test it, fix the problems, and eventually put it to work.

Of course, anyone who has spent much time developing software knows that the reality is considerably more complicated.

But there is another question that becomes especially important when the software is intended for scientific research.

What happens when the software works exactly as programmed, but the conclusions we draw from its results are wrong?

That question has become increasingly important in our Beyond the Light Barrier research.

We are developing BTLB-SIM, a computational framework intended to support investigations involving advanced communication, propulsion, spacetime physics, and other scientific questions.

Some of those investigations involve established physics. Others explore speculative possibilities that have not been experimentally demonstrated.

In either case, we need to know what our calculations actually establish.

And that means we cannot simply assume that our software architecture is trustworthy because we designed it carefully.

We have to challenge it.

Sometimes that means deliberately trying to break it.

Why Ordinary Testing Isn't Enough

Imagine developing a computer program that calculates the gravitational influence of a relativistic particle beam.

You write the equations, provide the parameters, and run the calculation.

The program produces a result.

You run it again. You get the same result.

You compare the result with another implementation, and the numbers agree.

That sounds encouraging.

But what have you actually established?

Perhaps both programs implemented the same incorrect equation.

Perhaps both relied on an assumption that does not apply to the physical situation.

Perhaps the numerical method was inappropriate.

Or perhaps the calculations were correct, but the result was interpreted as evidence of something the calculation never demonstrated.

These are different kinds of problems.

Software testing can help establish whether a program behaves according to its specifications.

Numerical verification can investigate whether a computation solves the specified equations to justified accuracy.

Scientific validation asks whether the model adequately represents the real-world phenomenon for its intended purpose.

Independent reproduction provides another opportunity to detect mistakes, hidden dependencies, and unsupported conclusions.

And a physical experiment introduces an entirely different category of evidence.

Success in one category does not automatically establish success in the others.

That distinction is fundamental to our research.

The Architecture Has Responsibilities Too

BTLB-SIM is intended to do more than calculate numbers.

We want it to support different scientific models and experiments without requiring us to rebuild the entire software system each time.

That means reusable components, defined interfaces, configurable experiments, and mechanisms for recording what happened.

But consider what those requirements imply.

Suppose an experiment produces an interesting result.

Months later, we want to understand exactly how that result was obtained.

We may need to reconstruct which model was used, which software version executed, what parameters were supplied, what numerical method was selected, and what happened during execution.

We also need to know which checks passed, which failed, and which questions remained unresolved.

If an execution was interrupted, did the system preserve enough information to understand its state?

If multiple operations occurred, did the records accurately preserve their ordering and relationships?

If a component failed, could the framework distinguish that failure from a failure in the scientific model?

These are not merely administrative questions.

They determine whether someone can audit, reproduce, and correctly interpret a computational result.

An architecture that loses important information may produce convincing output while leaving us unable to establish what that output means.

So We Decided to Attack Our Own Design

This led to the BTLB-SIM AR-1.7 Architecture Stress Audit.

The purpose was not to demonstrate that our architecture was correct.

It was to investigate where its assumptions, responsibilities, and execution behavior might fail.

Instead of asking only whether the software could perform expected operations, we examined difficult cases involving execution ordering, interruption, recovery, ownership, provenance, and the relationships between software operations and research records.

Some of these questions were surprisingly complicated.

Consider a system that records a sequence of operations.

Under ordinary conditions, the sequence may appear obvious.

But what if an operation creates additional work?

What if execution stops before that work is completed?

What if an operation partially succeeds?

What if the system must resume later?

What if the information needed to determine the correct next operation has already been discarded?

A simplified implementation might appear to work for the examples we originally imagined.

But that does not establish that it preserves the information required for every supported case.

This is exactly the kind of assumption we wanted to challenge.

What We Actually Found

Two examples from the audit illustrate why these questions matter.

In one test, we deliberately introduced a failure during publication.

The resulting observation showed that the publication head could still indicate COMPLETED after an injected failure, even though the stronger whole-publication guarantee being tested had not been satisfied.

Imagine a scientific computing system reporting that a result has been successfully preserved when the complete publication process has not actually finished.

That does not necessarily mean the scientific calculation was wrong.

But it raises an important question about whether the system's records accurately describe what happened.

In another test, a batch of records was rejected because of a late identity conflict.

The existing conflicting record remained protected.

That part mattered.

But the audit also observed that the ledger grew from one entry to eight despite the batch being rejected.

In other words, protecting an existing record was not the same as guaranteeing that a rejected batch left no partial additions.

These were documented software observations under specific test conditions.

They did not establish corruption of a scientific result.

They did reveal weaknesses relative to the stronger guarantees being investigated.

And that is precisely why we wanted to run the tests.

When Failure Is a Useful Result

One of the most important lessons from AR-1.7 is that finding problems does not necessarily mean an investigation has failed.

Sometimes finding a problem is the reason the investigation exists.

The audit preserved 64 distinct raw FAIL observation records, including repeated attempts and variations across macOS and Windows. Each preserved record was checked against its committed size and SHA-256 hash during our subsequent documentary verification.

Those observations supported eight open architectural findings.

The number 64 does not mean we discovered 64 independent defects.

Several observations documented repetitions or variations associated with the same underlying finding.

The separate frozen discovery inventory contained 30 cases: 20 PASS, eight FAIL, and two INCONCLUSIVE.

Those case outcomes and the 64 preserved observations represent different units of evidence and should not be confused.

On October 24, 2026, AR-1.7 reached what we call bounded investigative closure.

That is an important phrase.

It means the defined investigation reached its documented stopping point.

It does not mean every problem discovered during that investigation was resolved.

All eight findings remained open, with corrective obligations preserved.

Some corrective designs had received scoped acceptance during review, while others remained at REVISE.

But scoped acceptance of a corrective design was not acceptance of the overall architecture.

Architecture acceptance was not established.

Implementation readiness and authorization were not established.

And the audit did not validate any scientific theory or physical phenomenon.

Nevertheless, the investigation produced useful information.

We knew more about what our architecture could and could not yet justify.

That knowledge matters.

Why We Don't Just Fix Everything Immediately

This raises another reasonable question.

If the audit discovers problems, why not simply correct the software and move forward?

Sometimes that is the appropriate response.

But not every failure identifies an isolated programming mistake.

A problem may reveal that the architecture has assigned a responsibility to the wrong component.

Or that two components depend on assumptions that are incompatible.

Or that the information needed to make a decision was never preserved.

Fixing one symptom without understanding the underlying problem can make the system more complicated while leaving its fundamental weakness intact.

Our investigation therefore required discovery before correction, including preserving the original failure observations.

During the continuing AR-1.7 investigation, we also encountered a different kind of problem involving the recovery and re-examination of an earlier architectural inquiry.

That inquiry was known as CP107-R1.

The original CP107 Git history could not be recovered. We returned to a verified predecessor and performed a fresh inquiry.

That investigation reached a REVISE disposition consistent with the surviving original report.

The unresolved issue was whether a target identified at the source level could be justified as the same applicable target in the corresponding project context.

The necessary connection had not been established.

That did not prove the correspondence was impossible.

Nor did it demonstrate a production software defect.

It meant that an important justification remained incomplete.

The original Git history was still unavailable, and the fresh inquiry did not constitute independent reproduction of a scientific result.

This is another example of why we preserve the distinction between what was established and what remained uncertain.

A failed or incomplete approach can be valuable if it tells us which assumptions need further examination.

A failure that is quietly overwritten teaches us much less.

When the Investigation Challenges the Architecture Itself

The audit gave us evidence to ask a more fundamental question.

Which parts of our existing architecture were actually necessary, and which parts needed to justify their complexity?

That is a real challenge in engineering.

After spending considerable time developing a design, it is tempting to keep adding corrections and exceptions rather than reconsidering the design itself.

But the purpose of BTLB-SIM is not to defend an architectural idea.

Its purpose is to support trustworthy scientific research.

If the existing architecture can be corrected and simplified, we should consider that.

If its responsibilities need to be reorganized, we should consider that too.

If a hybrid design would work better, we should investigate it.

And if the evidence eventually supports replacing the architecture entirely, we should be willing to do that.

On October 24, 2026, I adopted the BTLB-SIM Next Architecture Exploration charter, known as NAE-1.

That charter gave us a framework for comparing possible architectural directions.

It permitted evolutionary improvements, redesign, a cohesive modular approach, multiple specialized architectures, hybrid solutions, and even a clean-sheet replacement.

The existing architecture remained a historical candidate, not an automatically preferred solution.

All eight open findings and their corrective obligations carried forward.

No replacement architecture was selected.

No implementation was authorized.

And the adoption review was a bounded internal documentary review, not independent scientific reproduction.

One way I would summarize our approach is this:

Preserve the obligation, not necessarily the implementation.

In other words, we should preserve the scientific and engineering requirements that matter without assuming that the original way of satisfying them must survive.

Are We Making the Software Too Complicated?

This is a question we need to keep asking.

There is a danger that a research project can become so involved in building its tools that it stops making progress on the questions those tools were supposed to investigate.

We do not want that.

But there is also a danger in making software simpler by ignoring responsibilities that matter.

For example, eliminating detailed execution records might make a program easier to develop.

But if those records are necessary to reproduce or interpret its results, the simplification may undermine the scientific purpose of the software.

The challenge is not to build the most elaborate architecture possible.

It is to build an architecture that is sufficiently reliable, understandable, and reproducible for the work it actually needs to perform.

The NAE-1 charter also allows us to consider whether particular scientific requirements would be better handled outside the simulator.

Sometimes a small, independently specified calculation may be more appropriate than an entire computational framework.

That possibility should be evaluated on its merits.

The method should fit the question.

What Does This Have to Do With Faster-Than-Light Research?

Quite a lot, although perhaps not in the way someone might initially expect.

Beyond the Light Barrier investigates questions where extraordinary claims could easily arise.

Could a particular spacetime geometry permit an unusual form of communication?

Could a proposed propulsion mechanism satisfy the relevant physical constraints?

Could an experimental measurement distinguish a predicted effect from ordinary backgrounds?

These questions require more than interesting numerical output.

They require clear assumptions, correct mathematics, appropriate numerical methods, and evidence that supports the conclusions being drawn.

The AR-1.7 tests told us how particular software mechanisms behaved under recorded conditions.

They did not establish that our scientific calculations were numerically reliable.

They did not validate the physical models.

And they did not reproduce a scientific result independently.

Those questions require separate investigations.

If a simulation produces an unexpected result, we need to investigate whether it reflects the physical model, the numerical method, the software implementation, or an error.

If a calculation contradicts accepted theory, that does not automatically mean we have discovered new physics.

It may mean we have discovered a mistake.

And if an investigation produces a negative result, we should preserve it rather than discard it because it is disappointing.

We are not trying to build software that confirms our favorite ideas. We are trying to build tools that can help us discover when those ideas are wrong.

That is a much more useful goal.

What Would Success Actually Look Like?

Success would not mean that BTLB-SIM never encounters a failure.

It would mean that the framework's supported responsibilities are clearly defined, its important behaviors are adequately verified, and its limitations are visible.

It would mean that a scientific result can be traced to its model, assumptions, implementation, parameters, and execution record.

It would mean that another investigator has enough information to challenge or reproduce the work.

It would mean that negative and inconclusive results are preserved alongside successful ones.

And it would mean that we are willing to replace parts of the system when the evidence shows a better approach is needed.

We are not there yet.

AR-1.7 identified important unresolved obligations.

NAE-1 is an exploration, not a completed architectural solution.

Those are the actual research states, and they should remain visible.

Closing Reflection

After decades of developing software, I am familiar with the satisfaction of seeing a complex system work.

But this research has reinforced something important.

There is a difference between making software work and establishing how much confidence we should place in what it tells us.

For Beyond the Light Barrier, that difference matters enormously.

We are investigating questions that may eventually lead to new experimental possibilities—or may reveal that certain approaches cannot work.

Either outcome can advance our understanding if the investigation is rigorous.

That is why we deliberately challenge our own architecture.

Not because we expect it to fail.

Not because failure is the objective.

But because we would rather discover an architectural weakness during a controlled investigation than mistake its consequences for a scientific discovery.

Before we ask our software to challenge the boundaries of physics, we want to make sure we have challenged the software itself.

And when it fails, we want to understand why.

That is how we make progress we can trust.

Research Status

Publication category: Research Explained — accessible interpretation of documented engineering and scientific-method investigations.

Established project findings: AR-1.7 reached bounded investigative closure on October 24, 2026, preserving 64 raw FAIL observation records supporting eight open findings. The separate 30-case inventory contained 20 PASS, eight FAIL, and two INCONCLUSIVE outcomes.

Architecture status: Overall architecture acceptance, implementation readiness, and implementation authorization were not established by AR-1.7.

Current architectural direction: NAE-1 was adopted October 24, 2026, as an architecture exploration charter. It inherited the eight open findings without selecting or authorizing a successor implementation.

Physical experimental status: This article reports no physical experiment, independently reproduced scientific result, or demonstration of faster-than-light communication or propulsion.

Sources & References

  1. Beyond the Light Barrier Research Method, v1.2 — project evidence classifications, reproducibility, negative-result preservation, and publication-integrity standards.
  2. BTLB Simulation Framework Implementation State, v0.9-dev — historical framework implementation checkpoint.
  3. BTLB-SIM AR-1.7 Final Bounded Closure, October 24, 2026, commit cee28d7a3016223e0f28b776683a780d77fd707e — final disposition, eight open findings, and investigation limitations.
  4. AR-1.7 Observation Portability Map and 64 preserved observation records, cp131/OBSERVATION-PORTABILITY-MAP.json and cp131/observations/, at the AR-1.7 closure commit — observation inventory and preserved failure evidence.
  5. BTLB-SIM CP107-R1 Portable Recovery and Comparison Records, semantic HEAD 8788ab584c84732119dfaa76280c37e4f8fc8fc1 — REVISE disposition, incomplete source/project target correspondence, and original-history recovery limitations.
  6. BTLB-SIM Next Architecture Exploration Charter, v1.0 — Adopted, October 24, 2026 — permitted alternatives, inherited corrective obligations, and architecture-selection boundaries.
  7. BTLB-SIM NAE-1 Adoption Record, v1.0 — October 24, 2026 — owner adoption and bounded documentary-review status.
  8. BTLB-RE24-PRIMARY-VERIFY-1 — Primary-Record Verification Report, November 2026 — documentary verification of V1–V7, including the claim-evidence matrix, 64 preserved observations, and eight-finding inventory. The report is retained in the project's research records; public access has not been established.

Research integrity note: This article reports documented software architecture investigations and their limitations. It does not establish that BTLB-SIM is fully verified, that a successor architecture has been accepted, that a scientific result has been independently reproduced, or that any speculative physical phenomenon has been experimentally demonstrated.

    mean we have discovered new physics.
  

  
It may mean we have discovered a mistake.

  

    And if an investigation produces a negative result, we should preserve it
    rather than discard it because it is disappointing.
  

  

    We are not trying to build software that confirms our favorite ideas. We
      are trying to build tools that can help us discover when those ideas are
      wrong.
  

  
That is a much more useful goal.

  
What Would Success Actually Look Like?

  
Success would not mean that BTLB-SIM never encounters a failure.

  

    It would mean that the framework's supported responsibilities are clearly
    defined, its important behaviors are adequately verified, and its
    limitations are visible.
  

  

    It would mean that a scientific result can be traced to its model,
    assumptions, implementation, parameters, and execution record.
  

  

    It would mean that another investigator has enough information to challenge
    or reproduce the work.
  

  

    It would mean that negative and inconclusive results are preserved alongside
    successful ones.
  

  

    And it would mean that we are willing to replace parts of the system when
    the evidence shows a better approach is needed.
  

  
We are not there yet.

  
AR-1.7 identified important unresolved obligations.

  
NAE-1 is an exploration, not a completed architectural solution.

  
Those are the actual research states, and they should remain visible.

  
Closing Reflection

  

    After decades of developing software, I am familiar with the satisfaction of
    seeing a complex system work.
  

  
But this research has reinforced something important.

  

    There is a difference between making software work and establishing how much
    confidence we should place in what it tells us.
  

  
For Beyond the Light Barrier, that difference matters enormously.

  

    We are investigating questions that may eventually lead to new experimental
    possibilities—or may reveal that certain approaches cannot work.
  

  

    Either outcome can advance our understanding if the investigation is
    rigorous.
  

  
That is why we deliberately challenge our own architecture.

  
Not because we expect it to fail.

  
Not because failure is the objective.

  

    But because we would rather discover an architectural weakness during a
    controlled investigation than mistake its consequences for a scientific
    discovery.
  

  

    Before we ask our software to challenge the boundaries of physics, we
      want to make sure we have challenged the software itself.
  

  
And when it fails, we want to understand why.

  
That is how we make progress we can trust.
